m1.q: Your suite runs 1,200 tests and it's all green. What can you state with certainty?
o: That your tests, as written, didn't find anything
You can sign off every user story in the sprint
m1.why: “All green” only speaks about your tests, not about the software. Signing off also requires evidence and traceability.

m1.q: Risk = probability × impact. With one afternoon available, what do you test FIRST?
o: The payment flow used by 90% of customers
A misaligned tooltip in the admin panel
A settings screen that gets used once a year
The alphabetical order of a list
m1.why: Risk-based testing: the highest probability×impact product goes first. Everything else waits.

m1.q: Your regression suite hasn't found a single bug in 6 months. What does the pesticide paradox say?
o: The app has no bugs left
You need to run it more often
The same tests stop finding new bugs: you have to review them and vary data/scenarios
You can delete the regression suite
m1.why: Repeated tests “immunize” the same path. You review and vary them; you don't assume health.

m1.q: “Exhaustive testing is impossible” (ISTQB principle). What does it mean in your day-to-day work?
o: That testing a lot isn't worth it
Prioritize by risk and impact: you decide WHAT to test because you can't test everything
That the happy path is enough
Hire more QAs until everything is covered
m1.why: A 10-character field already has more combinations than your sprint has seconds. The prioritization criteria IS the job.

m1.q: “Are we building the RIGHT product?” — is that verification or validation?
m1.why: Validation = the right product (it serves the user/business). Verification = the product built right (it meets the spec).

o: Because QAs charge less at the start of the project
Because a defect caught in requirements/design costs orders of magnitude less than in production
Because it moves the release date forward
m1.why: The cost of a defect grows over time: in production it means a hotfix, support and reputation. Catching it in the spec costs a conversation.

m1.q: You find that 80% of historical bugs live in 3 modules (defect clustering). What do you do?
o: Put extra effort there without neglecting the rest (because of the pesticide paradox)
m1.why: Clustering tells you where to bet more; the pesticide paradox reminds you not to abandon the rest of the map.

m1.q: What is a “charter” in session-based exploratory testing?
o: The session's mission: what to explore, with what focus and in how much time — plus notes on what was found
m1.why: Exploratory ≠ random clicking: it's a session with a mission, a timebox and notes. The charter is what makes it auditable.

m1.q: The app has had 0 reported bugs in 3 months, but users abandon it because it doesn't solve their problem. Which principle applies?
m1.why: “Absence of errors” doesn't guarantee value: a bug-free product that doesn't serve the business is still a failure. That's why validation exists.

m1.q: What is the difference between QA and QC?
o: QA improves the PROCESS to prevent defects; QC evaluates the PRODUCT to detect them
QC is manual and QA is automated
m1.why: QC finds the bug; QA asks why the process let it be born and how to prevent the next one. The modern role does both.

m30.q: Your suite has been green for months. What question does WAR ask?
o: What line coverage does it have?
Would the suite notice if I broke something on purpose?
m30.why: A guard who never shouts may be excellent or asleep. The only way to know is to break something on purpose and watch.

m30.q: In WAR, what does PASS mean?
o: That the mutation went through unseen
That the unmutated baseline behaves as the specification says, so the guard raises no false alarms
m30.why: PASS is about the baseline reality. What the guard catches is KILLED and what slips past it is SURVIVED.

m30.q: In experiment 01, run 3 without pins scores 76 against a gate of 70 and comes out REJECTED. Why?
o: Must criteria failed (AC-1 and AC-3), and a failing must blocks at any score
m30.why: Shoulds add to the score; musts block. An editor who approves their own draft isn't offset by points.

m30.q: Same input, three runs: approved, approved, rejected. What do you conclude?
o: Keep running until it comes out approved
The verdict is UNSTABLE, and that's a finding about the judge or the configuration, not about the story
m30.why: The score may move; the verdict may not. In 01 the set without pins (temperature 1, latest prompt) is the one that changes.

m30.q: Why does experiment 03 put the “no push to main” rule in a hook and not in the prompt?
o: Because a prompt can be ignored, while a PreToolUse hook that exits with code 2 always blocks the command
m30.why: Hard rules live in hooks and in CI. And like any guard, the hook is tested with attempts to sneak past it; one uncovered two real holes (git -c and git --no-pager), fixed in commit 1b01c66.

m30.q: The self-grant mutant survives in experiment 02. What kind of finding is it?
o: A blind spot in the suite: a test is missing
A real bug in the system: the app lets a user promote themselves to admin
m30.why: The mutant scenario records that the mutation was accepted with a 200. What's wrong is the app's editMember rule, and the README reports it as a real authorization bug.

m30.q: A very small numeric mutant survives with the tolerance frozen at 10⁻⁶. What do you do?
o: Report it as SURVIVED and leave it visible, without touching the tolerance
Lower the tolerance to kill it
m30.why: In scientific-qa-evidence the tiny RC mutation was deliberately left visible. Moving the tolerance after seeing the result is fitting to the result.

m30.q: Why must each mutant change exactly one thing?
o: So you can tell what the guard caught: with two changes you don't know which one made it shout
m30.why: One change, one attributable verdict. With several changes at once, a KILLED can hide that the guard doesn't see one of them.

m30.q: In the physics track, who judges the Snell mutation with the indices swapped?
o: The same solver that generated the data
An independent oracle with a frozen tolerance of 10⁻⁶
m30.why: If the oracle shared code or moved the tolerance, it would share the errors it's supposed to catch.

m30.q: What does a high kill rate NOT prove?
o: That the guard catches the mutations in the catalog
That the guard would catch mutations nobody wrote: the catalog carries its author's biases
m30.why: That's why the best mutants are planted by someone else, as in the blind tests of level 4.

m2.q: A field accepts integers from 1 to 100. Which set applies boundary value analysis BEST?
m2.why: The boundaries and their immediate neighbors (0/1 and 100/101) are where off-by-one errors live.

m2.q: The discount depends on 3 combined conditions (VIP, coupon, amount>100). Which technique reveals the cases you're missing?
m2.why: Combined conditions → decision table: 2³ combinations in plain sight and no orphan rule.

m2.q: Which of these defect reports is defensible?
o: Steps + expected vs actual + environment + evidence (logs/screenshot)
“It's the same as last week's bug”
m2.why: Without reproducible steps, expected vs actual and evidence, the defect is neither actionable nor defensible.

m2.q: An order goes DRAFT → PAID → SHIPPED. What test does the state transition technique bring that others miss?
o: The INVALID transitions: e.g. trying SHIPPED→DRAFT or paying twice
m2.why: The state diagram exposes the transitions that must NOT exist — that's where business logic bugs live.

m2.q: 4 parameters with 3 values each = 81 combinations. What does pairwise give you?
o: A small subset that covers every PAIR of values — most interaction bugs involve 2 parameters
It removes the need for other techniques
m2.why: Empirical evidence: most interaction defects are triggered by pairs, not quadruples. Pairwise gives ~9-12 cases instead of 81.

m2.q: A typo in the home page title: “Welcomme”. Severity and priority?
m2.why: Minimal technical impact (low severity) but visible to every user (high fix priority). They're independent axes.

m2.q: Age field: valid from 18 to 65. What are the equivalence partitions?
m2.why: Partitions = classes where the system should behave the same: one valid and the invalid ones around it (plus the invalid data type).

m2.q: What feeds “error guessing” so it isn't pure guesswork?
o: Past experience, historical bugs and typical failure patterns of the team/domain
m2.why: It's an experience-based technique: it complements (doesn't replace) the systematic ones, and gets better the better you know the history.

m2.q: Which of these is a WELL-written test case?
o: Precondition + data + numbered steps + observable expected result
A video of the correct flow
m2.why: If someone else can't run it and decide pass/fail without asking you, it's not a test case: it's an intention.

m2.q: Which of these scenarios is NOT worth automating?
o: The smoke test for every deploy
m2.why: Automation costs maintenance: it pays off through repetition. What runs once and needs human judgment is done exploratory.

m3.q: Why open PRs with yourself in the course repo?
o: To rehearse the real flow (branch→PR→review→merge) and leave an auditable history
Because main is protected by default
To create merge conflicts on purpose
m3.why: The PR flow is the daily ritual of the craft; practicing it from day 0 makes it second nature on a team.

m3.q: You added invalid-credential cases to login. What's the correct conventional commit?
m3.why: type(scope): description — the history becomes a readable, automatable changelog.

m3.q: What goes in the README of an automation repo?
o: How to install, how to run each suite and how to read the report
m3.why: The README is onboarding: someone new (or the AI) must be able to run the suite without asking you.

m3.q: What exactly does “git checkout -b feat/login-tests” do?
o: Creates a new branch from where you are AND switches you to it
Creates the branch on the remote
m3.why: -b = create + switch in one step. The branch only exists locally until you push -u origin.

m3.q: Why is a 200-line PR reviewed better than a 2,000-line one?
o: Because the reviewer can sustain real attention: giant diffs get approved out of fatigue and bugs slip through
No difference if the code is good
m3.why: Review quality nosedives with size. Small, frequent PRs = real feedback, not an exhausted “LGTM”.

m3.q: What should be in a Playwright repo's .gitignore?
m3.why: Dependencies and run artifacts are regenerated; committing them bloats the repo and creates pointless conflicts.

m3.q: What's the difference between “npx playwright test” and having Playwright installed globally?
o: npx runs the project's LOCAL binary (the package.json version) — everyone runs the same version
npx always downloads the latest version
m3.why: The version is pinned by the project's lockfile, not by each person's machine. Goodbye “my machine runs a different version”.

m3.q: Merge conflict in a steps file. What do you do?
o: Understand BOTH changes and combine what belongs — both intentions may need to coexist
Delete the file and rewrite it
m3.why: Resolving blindly throws away someone else's work or your own. A conflict is a conversation between two intentions: read it.

m3.q: You bumped the Playwright version in package.json. What type of conventional commit is it?
m3.why: It doesn't add functionality or fix a product bug: it's project maintenance → chore/build depending on the team's convention.

m3.q: Why review your OWN diff before asking for review?
o: You catch your own obvious slips (forgotten logs, comments, extra files) and respect the reviewer's time
m3.why: The first review is yours: your own diff read with a reviewer's eyes filters 80% of the noise before bothering anyone else.

m3b.q: “Give enough context, not all of it.” In practice it means:
o: Pasting the whole vault into every prompt
Pointing to the relevant vault note
Giving no context so as not to bias the AI
Relying only on the chat history
m3b.why: Targeted context: the right note guides; dumping everything dilutes and burns the window.

m3b.q: According to the 3 layers of context, where do the PROJECT's rules live?
m3b.why: CLAUDE.md = project rules · memory = facts about you · Obsidian = deep knowledge.

m3b.q: You want something to happen ALWAYS when X happens (e.g. when saving a file). According to the method, that is:
o: A hook — “whatever you want to happen every time X”
m3b.why: What must happen on its own gets configured (hook); what depends on human memory fails.

m3b.q: You write [[contrato-pagos]] and the note doesn't exist yet. What is that?
o: An error to fix right away
Pending knowledge flagged: the broken link tells you what's left to document
m3b.why: In a living vault, a link to a future note is a work marker, not a bug. The graph shows you the gaps.

m3b.q: You solved a really weird bug after 4 hours. What do you document in the vault?
o: Root cause + solution + context (how it's detected, how it's prevented) — a note you or the AI can reuse
m3b.why: The 4 hours are paid once if they're distilled into a note. Without a note, the next person (or you in 6 months) pays them again.

m3b.q: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol) in one sentence?
o: A standard protocol for connecting tools and data sources to the AI model
m3b.why: MCP is the “USB of AI”: it exposes tools (browser, DB, APIs) for the model to use — key in the QA+AI stack.

m3b.q: What must NEVER go in the repo's CLAUDE.md?
m3b.why: CLAUDE.md is versioned with the repo and any tool reads it: secrets go in secret managers, never in versioned files.

m3b.q: “AI without context is a brilliant intern with amnesia.” Which part does persistent memory solve?
o: The amnesia: facts about you and how you work that survive across sessions
m3b.why: Each layer tackles amnesia at one level: memory = who you are; CLAUDE.md = what the project is like; vault = what the team knows.

m3b.q: What sets LIVING documentation apart from dead documentation?
o: It's updated as part of daily work and lives where you work — dead docs were written once for an auditor
m3b.why: Docs that aren't touched when the system changes start lying within weeks. Living docs are part of the flow: you change something, you update the note.

m3b.q: You need the AI to write tests for the payments API. What's the best input?
o: Pasting the vault note with the contract + dataset caveats as prompt context
Asking it to infer it from the endpoint names
m3b.why: The distilled note is quality context: the real contract + known traps. From memory = invented assumptions stated with confidence.

m4.q: Why is async/await critical in Playwright?
o: Almost the whole API returns Promises: without await you get false greens
m4.why: An expect without await can “pass” before the action finishes: a false green, your worst enemy.

m4.q: const r = await api.get<User>("/user/1"). What does the generic <User> give you?
o: It validates the response at runtime
Static typing (autocomplete and compile-time errors), but it does NOT validate at runtime
It turns the JSON into a User class
It throws if the service omits a field
m4.why: Types are erased at compile time. To validate the contract at runtime you need Zod/AJV (module 7).

m4.q: Why use a typed test data builder/factory?
o: Valid data by default + explicit variations per case, without duplicating objects
m4.why: user().withEmailInvalido() states the case's intent; copy/pasting JSON hides what varies.

m4.q: You receive external JSON. “any” or “unknown” to type it, and why?
o: unknown: it FORCES you to validate/narrow before using it — any turns the type-checker off
never, because you don't trust it
m4.why: any is a hole: everything compiles and nothing gets checked. unknown turns “I don't know what this is” into mandatory checking.

m4.q: You need data from 3 independent endpoints to build the test state. How do you request them?
o: await a(); await b(); await c(); — one after another
m4.why: If they don't depend on each other, running them in series adds up latencies for nothing. Promise.all overlaps them: 3×300ms ≈ 300ms, not 900ms.

m4.q: Why “strict: true” in a test framework's tsconfig?
o: It catches nulls/undefined and implicit types AT COMPILE TIME — framework bugs that would be flaky at runtime
m4.why: A test framework with strictNullChecks turned off hides exactly the class of errors you later call “flakiness”.

m4.q: “type Role = 'admin' | 'editor' | 'viewer'” — what does that union buy you?
o: A typo like 'editr' blows up at COMPILE time, not 20 minutes into a suite run
It validates the roles against the backend
m4.why: String literals close the universe of values: the compiler is your first test, and it runs in milliseconds.

m4.q: if (typeof x === "string") { x.toUpperCase() } — why does it compile without error if x was unknown?
o: Narrowing: inside the if, TS already knows x is a string
It doesn't compile: it's an error
m4.why: The type guard narrows the type in that scope. It's the pattern for working with unknown safely.

m4.q: An async test calls saveUser() without await and the test finishes green before the save fails. What is that bug called?
o: Floating promise: the error is lost and the green is false
m4.why: Every Promise must be awaited or handled. The no-floating-promises lint rule exists exactly for this — turn it on.

m4.q: Interface or type for a test's data object?
o: Either one: for data objects they're interchangeable; the team picks ONE convention
m4.why: The differences (declaration merging, unions) rarely matter for test data. What matters is converging on a single canonical form.

m5.q: A test fails intermittently: “sometimes the button isn't there”. The method's first move?
o: Correct locator + web-first assertions (auto-waiting) and check the trace
m5.why: sleep and retries cover it up; auto-waiting with the right locator cures it. The trace tells you what really happened.

o: Reusing the authenticated session instead of repeating the UI login in every test
m5.why: Log in once, persist the session, fast and stable tests. The UI login is tested once, separately.

m5.q: You need to validate the “order created” screen. How do you set up the state?
o: Creating the order through the UI in every test
Creating it through the API and validating through the UI (hybrid)
With a fixture that wipes the database
m5.why: Setting up through the API is fast and stable; the UI is reserved for what you actually want to validate.

m5.q: Why is getByRole("button", {name:"Pagar"}) a better locator than ".btn-pay-2 > span"?
o: It anchors to accessible semantics (what the user SEES) and survives CSS/structure refactors
m5.why: CSS changes every sprint; the role and accessible name only change if the product changes. Plus you validate accessibility for free.

m5.q: What's the difference between “await expect(loc).toBeVisible()” and “expect(await loc.isVisible()).toBe(true)”?
o: The first RETRIES until the timeout (web-first assertion); the second checks ONCE and fails if it hasn't loaded yet
m5.why: Web-first assertions are the antidote to flakiness: they wait for the condition to hold instead of snapshotting a single instant.

m5.q: What does a Playwright fixture give you compared to a global beforeEach?
o: Typed, composable, on-demand setup/teardown: each test declares what it needs and doesn't pay for what it doesn't use
m5.why: A fixture is dependency injection for tests: “this test needs an admin user” reads in the signature, not in some magic global setup.

m5.q: A test fails only in CI. Which tool shows you what happened step by step, with DOM, network and console?
o: The trace viewer (trace: "on-first-retry" + npx playwright show-trace)
m5.why: The trace is the flight's black box: DOM snapshots per action, requests and console. Debugging CI without a trace is guessing.

m5.q: Two parallel tests create the user “test@demo.com” and one fails randomly with “already exists”. What's the method's fix?
o: Unique data per test (faker/timestamp) or per-worker isolation: tests must not share mutable state
Wipe the DB before the suite
m5.why: Parallelism demands isolation. Serializing punishes the whole suite for a bad data design; the retry only hides the collision.

m5.q: You want to test how the UI looks when the backend returns a 500. How do you make it stable?
o: page.route() intercepting the endpoint and responding 500 (route.fulfill)
Wait for it to fail on its own
m5.why: Network interception simulates the failure on demand, deterministically and without touching shared environments. That's how you test unhappy paths.

m5.q: Why does every Playwright test run in a new browser context?
o: Isolation: clean cookies/storage per test — no test depends on the state another one left behind
So the video is kept separate
m5.why: Isolation is what enables parallelism and makes a red mean “this test found something”, not “the previous test left a mess”.

m6.q: The API returns “user_name” but the contract says “username”. The PO pushes you to unblock it. What do you do?
o: Change my schema to user_name so it passes
Accept both names with a oneOf
Revalidate against the LATEST version of the contract and report with evidence (cURL + response)
m6.why: First revalidate (a new version may settle the question); if it persists, report it. Adapting the test = masking.

m6.q: What's the difference between “aligning to the contract” and “masking”?
o: Aligning = updating the test because the CONTRACT changed; masking = loosening the test to cover up a violation
Aligning = adapting the schema to the observed response
m6.why: Direction matters: the contract rules over the test; the observed response does NOT rule over the schema.

m6.q: What does Zod/AJV give you that expect(r.status).toBe(200) doesn't?
o: Runtime validation of the WHOLE schema (types, required fields, formats): the schema IS the contract
m6.why: A 200 with a broken body is a false green. Typed schema validation is the real contract test.

m6.q: Your token is valid but you try to delete ANOTHER user's resource. What status code do you expect?
m6.why: 401 = I don't know who you are (authentication); 403 = I know who you are and you can't (authorization). Mixing them up hides RBAC bugs.

m6.q: You resend the same PUT /user/5 three times because of a network retry. What do you expect if the endpoint is correct?
o: The same final state: PUT must be idempotent
A 409 error on the second one
m6.why: Idempotency: N identical calls = same result. It's a key test case because network retries DO happen in production.

m6.q: When do you use PATCH instead of PUT?
o: PATCH = PARTIAL update (only the fields sent); PUT = full replacement of the resource
PATCH is the new version of PUT
m6.why: Testing a PATCH as if it were a PUT (or vice versa) produces false reds/greens: the verb's semantics are part of the contract.

m6.q: You're testing a paginated endpoint (?page=N&limit=M). Which set of cases follows the method?
o: page=1, last page, out-of-range page, limit=0 and limit>max, and stable ordering across pages
Only a huge limit to stress it
m6.why: Pagination breaks at the edges: empty page, out of range, invalid limits and items repeated/lost between pages.

m6.q: Your test sends an expired JWT and gets a 401. What is it?
o: The correct behavior: it's an expected NEGATIVE case of the auth contract
m6.why: Negative cases validate that the system rejects properly. A 401 for an expired token is a green for the negative case, not a failure.

m6.q: Do errors (4xx/5xx) have a contract too?
o: Yes: the structure of the error body (code, message, details) — and it's validated with a schema just like the 200s
m6.why: Consumers parse errors. A malformed error breaks integrations just like a broken 200 — validate them with Zod/AJV too.

m6.q: Where does the Zod schema that validates the response come from: the OpenAPI spec or a real response you captured?
o: From the real response: it's what there is
From the OpenAPI/contract: the spec is the source of truth — deriving the schema from the observed response institutionalizes masking
m6.why: If the schema is born from the response, it will always pass: you just turned the bug into the reference. The contract is the bible.

m7.q: Which of these steps is declarative Gherkin (the correct one)?
o: When I click "#btn-submit" and wait 2 seconds
When I submit the sign-up form with valid data
When I run window.submit() in the console
When the QA runs the sign-up test
m7.why: Declarative = business intent. Selectors, waits and technicalities live in the steps, not in the feature.

m7.q: When does BDD get in the way instead of helping?
o: When the business takes part in the examples
When the feature generates living documentation
When you use it as a technical wrapper with no business language: an extra layer with no value
m7.why: BDD without a business conversation is bureaucracy: you maintain two layers to read the same thing.

m7.q: Two devs wrote different families of steps that do the same thing. What does the method do?
o: Converge on ONE canonical form and refactor the features toward it
Create a third one better than both
m7.why: “A single canonical form”: duplicated steps break reuse — the core value of BDD.

m7.q: You have to test login with 5 credential combinations. Which Gherkin construct do you use?
m7.why: The Outline parametrizes the SAME behavior with different data: one template, N rows, zero duplication.

m7.q: Every scenario in the feature needs “Given I am logged in as admin”. Where does it go?
o: In a Background at the start of the feature
m7.why: Background = the feature's common preconditions, written once. Repeating them is noise; hiding them in hooks is invisible magic.

o: Selecting subsets at run time: smoke on every PR, regression nightly, one module on demand
m7.why: Tags are the selective execution system: without them, you either run everything every time or edit code to filter.

m7.q: You see “Then the response contains $.data.items[0].status == ACTIVE” in a feature. Diagnosis?
o: Technical detail in the business layer: the JSONPath goes INSIDE the step; the feature says “the order shows as active”
m7.why: The business reads the feature. The verification mechanics (JSONPath, schemas) are the step's implementation, not ubiquitous language.

m7.q: Who are “the 3 amigos” and when do they meet?
o: QA, senior dev and junior dev, at the retro
Business/PO, dev and QA — BEFORE building, to agree on concrete examples of the behavior
PO, scrum master and manager, at refinement
m7.why: BDD is born from that early conversation: the agreed examples become scenarios. Without it, BDD is just syntax.

m7.q: What is “living documentation” in a BDD pipeline?
o: A wiki someone updates on Fridays
The report generated on every run: the scenarios in business language + their real current status
m7.why: Since the scenarios ARE executable, the report says what the system does TODAY — documentation that can't lie.

o: By business behavior/capability (checkout.feature, returns.feature), not by screen or technical class
By the sprint they were written in
m7.why: The feature mirrors the domain, not the architecture. If a technical refactor forces you to move features, they were badly organized.

m7b.q: 7 out of 120 failed in cycle 1. The fix arrives. What do you run in cycle 2?
o: Only the 7 that failed; the full regression ONCE at the end
Nothing until they confirm the fix in QA
m7b.why: “Iterate narrow, confirm wide”: retest what failed, and one full regression at the close — not on every round.

m7b.q: A deactivated record returns 204 with an empty body and your test marks it as a failure. What is it?
o: A special dataset state that should be documented — the test must account for it
m7b.why: Data in a special state isn't a bug. The dataset is documented with its caveats — “no data, nothing runs”.

m7b.q: What ALWAYS comes with a valid @IGNORE?
o: A comment with the ticket (which stays Open), an explicit condition for removing it, and the user story does NOT close
m7b.why: An @IGNORE with no ticket and no exit condition is a buried bug with a nice tombstone.

m7b.q: Put the method's cycle protocol in order:
o: New → fix → retest ONLY what failed → full regression at the end (once)
m7b.why: The order exists so you don't pay for the full regression on every round: narrow to iterate, wide to close.

m7b.q: “No data, nothing runs.” What does it imply BEFORE starting a cycle?
o: Prepared and documented datasets (with an owner and caveats) as a precondition of the cycle — not as a mid-run surprise
Asking the dev for data when something fails
m7b.why: Half the “failures” of a poorly prepared cycle are missing data or data in an unexpected state. Data is a prior deliverable.

m7b.q: An entity has a 1→N relationship with its documents. What cases does the cardinality demand?
o: With 0 documents, with 1, and with MANY — each of the three states breaks differently
Doesn't matter: the relationship belongs to the backend
m7b.why: 0 breaks renders and validations, 1 is the happy path, N breaks pagination/performance/aggregations. Cardinality is test data design.

o: At the next regression, just in case
When the documented condition is met (e.g. the vendor's fix deployed and verified) — then the scenario goes back into the run
When the ticket is a month old
m7b.why: The tag carries its exit condition in writing. Without a verifiable condition, the @IGNORE becomes permanent and the coverage lied.

m7b.q: The retest of the 7 failures passed, but the final regression broke 2 tests in ANOTHER module. What does it mean?
o: The fix had side effects: this is exactly what the final regression is for — report it as a new defect linked to the fix
Nothing, if the retest passed it's closed
m7b.why: “Confirm wide” exists because fixes break things far from where they touch. That finding is the regression paying for itself.

m7b.q: In a shared environment, your test assumes the demo user has 3 orders and today it has 7. What's the lesson?
o: Ask that nobody else use the environment
Don't assume state: create the data you need (or reserve your own datasets) and clean up on the way out
Run only in the early morning
m7b.why: Shared environments are hostile by definition. A test that assumes someone else's state is flaky by design, not by bad luck.

m7b.q: What's the difference between retest and regression?
o: Retest = confirming THE specific failure was fixed; regression = confirming nothing else broke with the change
m7b.why: They answer different questions: “is it fixed?” vs “what did the fix break?”. Confusing them leaves holes in the cycle's close.
